criterion.summary: No single numerical threshold. GW150914 and GW151226 qualify via FAR < 1 per 50,000 yr; LVT151012 via p_astro = 0.976 / TDR 99.92% in a selected BBH region. The paper calls exactly these three 'statistically significant' and the BBH table caption draws the line at a TDR threshold of 99.92%.
criterion.quote: There are three candidates which are statistically significant. These are the binary black hole mergers GW150914, LVT151012, and GW151226, which were previously reported in~\cite{TheLIGOScientific:2016pea,Abbott:2016blz,Abbott:2016nmj}. [...] There are no other individually convincing candidates.

supporting_quotes.section: Sec. 3 Evaluating Candidates based on the Astrophysical Population
supporting_quotes.quote: We find two candidate events with FAR $< 1$ per $50\,000$ years, corresponding to GW150914 and GW151226.

There are three binary black hole mergers above a threshold corresponding to a true discovery rate of $99.92\%$. The third most significant event, LVT151012, has a 97.6\% probability of being astrophysical in origin.
Given a \pastro{} value of 97.6$\%$ we conclude that LVT151012 is astrophysical in origin.

We independently verify the discovery of GW150914 and GW151226 and report an improved significance of the candidate event LVT151012, which we claim should be viewed as a confident detection.  Apart from these three signals, none of the other candidate events are individually significant in our analysis.

tiers.name: FAR < 1 per 50,000 yr (GW150914, GW151226)
tiers.quote: We find two candidate events with FAR $< 1$ per $50\,000$ years, corresponding to GW150914 and GW151226.

tiers.name: LVT151012 via p_astro/TDR in selected BBH region
tiers.quote: We combine this FAR  with our conservative estimate of the rate of detections to estimate that 99.92\% of binary black hole merger candidates at least as significant as LVT151012 are astrophysical in origin. We also estimate the probability that specifically LVT151012 is astrophysical in origin to be 97.59$\%$.

tiers.name: sub-threshold (no other tier named)
tiers.quote: The fourth event has only a 6$\%$ chance of being astrophysical.

events.gps_source: computed from Julian Date column (2457279.910665, Tables 1-2). The JD is on the TAI scale, not UTC: treating it as UTC (+17 s) disagrees with the UTC time in the designation by 36 s (= TAI-UTC), so GPS = (JD-2444244.5)*86400 - 19 s. Check: the result matches the UTC time in the designation +17 s. JD has 6 decimals, so precision is ~0.09 s
events.notes: GW150914 and GW151226 established by FAR < 1 per 50,000 yr (Sec. 3); assumed signals in TDR/p_astro construction so no p_astro reported ("-").

new_detection_claim.quote: Since no new astrophysical events have been observed, we do not consider measurement of the signals' parameters
other_quotes: No other astrophysically significant signals are observed. (Sec. 1)
No other significant binary black hole candidates are found, nor did we observe any significant binary neutron star or neutron star--black hole candidates. (Abstract)
new_detection_claim.note: Its only upgrade is LVT151012 (LVC: candidate, not an unambiguous detection) to 'should be considered a true astrophysical event' (Sec. 1). No GW-named event outside LVC O1 results.

open_questions: No uniform numerical detection threshold: GW150914/GW151226 qualify by FAR, LVT151012 by p_astro/TDR in a restricted BBH region; p_astro is not reported for the top two.

GPS times are not tabulated; computed from the 6-decimal Julian Date (~0.09 s resolution). The JD column is evidently TAI-scale (36 s ahead of the designation UTC), so GPS = (JD-2444244.5)*86400 - 19; under a UTC reading the result would be 36 s off.
Paper never writes 'GW151012'; LVT151012 is the only GW-style name for that event.
